documents.abstract: Virtual immersive learning platforms (VILPs), integrating immersive technologies, gamified design, and learning tools, enable meaningful engagement in learning while also creating possibilities for compulsive engagement. Drawing on a sociotechnical affordance perspective, this study examines how configurations of affordances are associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and how these pathways vary across demographic conditions. Using a mixed-methods design, we first uncover the core affordances of VILPs and organize them within a sociotechnical perspective. We then employ a two-stage fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine affordance configurations associated with different engagement outcomes and the role of demographic conditions. The findings show that meaningful and compulsive engagement are associated with distinct combinations of affordances and these configurational patterns vary across demographic conditions. These findings advance understanding of VILP engagement by revealing the configurational pathways associated with meaningful and compulsive engagement and offering practical insights into designing more inclusive and responsible learning platforms.

Generative artificial intelligence has introduced new forms of assistance, automation, and co-production in teaching, intensifying debates about teacher agency, pedagogical judgment, and professional autonomy. This study aimed to characterize the evolution, thematic structure, and research fronts connecting teacher agency with generative artificial intelligence between 2022 and 10 September 2026. An exploratory bibliometric analysis was conducted on a verified corpus of 30 DOI-bearing publications retrieved through structured searches of open scholarly metadata and cross-checked against publisher records. Temporal productivity, source concentration, conceptual recurrence, and thematic relationships were examined. Output was absent in 2022, incipient in 2023-2024, and accelerated in 2025-2026, which accounted for 80.0% of the corpus. Mapping identified four clusters: agency and professional judgment, teacher education, professional knowledge for AI integration, and assessment-governance. Recent literature shifts attention from technology adoption toward negotiated control, critical validation of algorithmic outputs, and preservation of professional responsibility. The field is therefore in an early consolidation phase, characterized by fragmented authorship and increasing conceptual convergence around human-AI relations. Future research should expand longitudinal evidence, include Latin American contexts, and examine institutional conditions that strengthen or constrain teacher agency.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract This research note introduces the proposed designation Agentic Delegation Charter (ADC), alongside its French equivalent, Charte de délégation agentique, within the research programme of Blooming Semantics Institute (BSI). Drawing on established project management principles, the proposal outlines a governance framework for successive delegations involving artificial intelligence agents. Three interdependent principles are identified: recursive project governance, whereby each successive delegation is treated as a subordinate project subject to the overarching charter; terminological invariance and semantic continuity, supported by an authoritative project-specific lexicon; and distributed authority, governed through explicit conditions of authorization, competence, accountability, and control. The note also identifies challenges concerning semantic interpretation, the evolution of delegated authority, human oversight, and the temporal constraints of decision-making. Its purpose is to document a preliminary terminological and conceptual proposal dated 16 October 2026, without claiming exclusive authorship of the expression or establishing scientific originality prior to a comprehensive review of the literature.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Industrial visual inspection requires not only accurate segmentation but also reliable and traceable decision making, since incorrect automatic refinements may lead to downstream manufacturing failures. Although segmentation foundation models achieve strong segmentation accuracy, they provide limited support for assessing whether refinement actions should be accepted, rejected, or escalated before deployment. To address this challenge, we propose AgenticInspect, a hybrid-audited agentic inspection framework that reformulates segmentation refinement as an action-level, risk-aware decision process. AgenticInspect treats an edge-deployable segmentation model as a replaceable skill. Based on the output of the segmentation skill, AgenticInspect introduces three task-specific decision modules, including uncertainty- and geometry-guided candidate generation, train-learned gating for high-risk refinement actions, and hybrid audit for risk-controlled mask selection. The hybrid audit layer integrates deterministic safety rules, train-learned safety gates, and selective large language model (LLM) review. The proposed framework provides action-level risk control and auditable decision making, with a traceable rationale for accepting, rejecting, or escalating candidate refinements. AgenticInspect was evaluated on a labeled connector-inspection dataset. The proposed refinement pipeline improved IoU from 0.9189303 to 0.9190180. The full hybrid policy reduced degraded refinements from 14 to 12 while maintaining nearly all performance gains (IoU = 0.9190131). Audit-component ablation attributes the observed reduction in IoU-degrading outputs to the train-learned risk veto, while LLM review serves as a selective, structured, and auditable assistive interface rather than an independently validated source of automatic improvement. These results position AgenticInspect as a risk-aware inspection framework that converts static segmentation outputs into auditable refinement decisions.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association. Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.

Tool-using LLM agents repeatedly face decision points under uncertainty, choosing between autonomous action, additional information gathering, and human escalation. These decisions require balancing task success against interaction cost and the risk of irreversible errors. Learning to make these trade-offs is challenging because existing interaction trajectories record only the outcomes of actions taken, leaving the consequences of alternative actions unobserved. To address this gap, we construct a counterfactual dataset containing 3,115 action outcomes from 1,036 decision points in ToolSandbox. At each decision point, we execute each legal action and evaluate its downstream outcomes based on task completion, interaction cost, and irreversible errors. Using this dataset, we train SURE-Act, a controller that selects actions for a frozen backbone agent at inference time. Our experiments show that learning to rank alternative actions improves offline action-selection utility by 0.0309 over a regression-only baseline. We further show that adding SURE-Act enables end-to-end gains of up to 0.0575 in ToolSandbox's Overall Score with the Qwen3-4B agent. Moreover, SURE-Act outperforms adapted decision rules from SAGE-Agent and Calibrate-Then-Act by 0.1506 and 0.1438, respectively. This work establishes the first counterfactual dataset for ToolSandbox and provides actionable insights into decision-making under uncertainty for tool-using agents.

AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent digital actors that can reason, access enterprise knowledge, invoke tools, and execute business actions. Unlike conventional applications, agents may adapt their behavior dynamically and operate with varying levels of autonomy, making lifecycle governance essential. This paper proposes an AI Agent Lifecycle Governance Framework covering ideation, risk classification, design, data and model selection, identity, tool approval, development, testing, security review, Responsible AI evaluation, deployment, runtime monitoring, change management, recertification, suspension, and retirement. The framework integrates enterprise architecture, model risk management, cybersecurity, auditability, human oversight, and operational governance into a repeatable lifecycle. It defines governance gates, accountable roles, evidence requirements, runtime controls, and measurable KPIs/KRIs. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale agentic AI responsibly while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, regulatory readiness, and long-term operational control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Advanced AI technologies and analytics inform critical decisions within contemporary corporate strategies. Existing research underscores the advantages of using artificial intelligence for operations and analysis but lacks comprehensive insights into how these systems affect overall strategy formulation, business flexibility, and leadership performance in various sectors. In pursuit of filling this void, our current research investigates how machine learning, predictive analysis, natural language handling, and automated systems contribute significantly to improving business strategies. This analysis explores how companies utilize vast amounts of information to predict changes in markets, enhance their processes, elevate service quality for customers, and secure an edge over rivals. Drawing upon examples from sectors like retail, health care, manufacturing, and finance, this document demonstrates how artificial intelligence enhances business strategies through real-world applications. Additionally, this research examines significant obstacles including issues related to personal information security, discrimination in machine learning models, moral considerations, and the necessity of efficient cooperation between humans and artificial intelligence systems. Evidence highlights the significance of cultivating data-centric environments, enhancing technological frameworks, and nurturing leaders adept at guiding AI-informed organizational shifts. In summary, this study offers a comprehensive view of how artificial intelligence and digital ecosystems facilitate agile, robust, and insightful approaches within evolving corporate landscapes.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Chapter 7 explores how artificial intelligence is transforming the architecture, culture and governance of modern organisations, revealing both the risks and opportunities of technological acceleration. It argues that AI does not simply automate existing processes but fundamentally reshapes how work is organised, how decisions are made and how value is created. Drawing on the author’s experience redesigning an advisory organisation at Human Planet, the chapter illustrates how AI can invert traditional hierarchical structures, replacing labour-intensive pyramids with lean, purpose-driven systems where experienced professionals are supported by intelligent tools. In this model, technology handles complexity and repetition, while humans focus on judgement, creativity and service. Beyond structural efficiency, the chapter examines the cultural and ethical implications of AI adoption. It highlights how intelligent systems can restore human-centred productivity by removing administrative burdens, enabling organisations to redirect energy towards meaning, collaboration and innovation. At the same time, the chapter warns that AI amplifies the values embedded in an organisation: when guided by vocation and ethical leadership, it strengthens transparency, accountability and stakeholder empowerment; when misaligned, it risks accelerating bias, opacity and institutional failure. Ultimately, Chapter 7 positions artificial intelligence not as a substitute for purpose but as a catalyst that makes organisational vocation more actionable, reinforcing the central premise of the vocating framework: that technology must serve human dignity, long-term stewardship and meaningful contribution.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes virtually every field, universities face a growing imperative to ensure AI literacy is not reserved for computer science majors alone. This panel presents the collaborative design of an introductory AI course built for undergraduate general education — one that serves students across disciplines, regardless of technical background. Two co-designers will share the story of building the course from complementary angles. The first presenter will address the technical foundation of the curriculum: how core AI concepts such as machine learning, data, and algorithms were translated into accessible, hands-on learning experiences for non-specialist students. The second presenter will explore the philosophical framework woven throughout the course — examining questions of ethics, agency, bias, and what it means to be human in an age of intelligent machines. The panelists will discuss how technical and philosophical threads were intentionally integrated rather than siloed, creating a course where students not only understand how AI works, but are equipped to think critically about why it matters. Attendees will come away with practical insights on curriculum structure, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and strategies for making AI education inclusive for students from diverse academic and experiential backgrounds. This session is designed for faculty, instructional designers, and administrators interested in developing or expanding AI literacy offerings at their institutions.
topics: Interdisciplinary Studies: Technology, Society, and Humanities

documents.abstract: AI has taken the academic world by storm, dramatically affecting written assignments and student performance evaluations. This paper examines the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) from the teaching perspective, with emphasis on daily grading workflows. We analyze benefits such as fair and consistent application of rubrics, the ability to incorporate articles and course materials as inputs to grading, and the delivery of individualized, extensive feedback. We compare these capabilities against a representative product—EssayGrader—situate our claims within current scholarship on Automated Essay Scoring (AES) and Large Language Models (LLMs) as graders, and provide policy guidance.

Chapter 5 reframes artificial intelligence (AI) as an operational capability within a learning health system rather than as a collection of models or demonstrations. AI creates value only when an output is connected to a threshold, named owner, funded response capacity, executable workflow, and continuous monitoring. The chapter maps eight operational roles – sensing and capture; synthesis and communication; prediction and prioritization; decision support; standardization and legitimation; automation and orchestration; enactment in practice; and monitoring, learning, and governance – across the five transformations from Practice to Data through Routines to Practice. Kaiser Permanente’s Advance Alert Monitor provides the principal case, showing how remote nurse review and rapid-response pathways converted deterioration scores into earlier intervention and improved outcomes. Supporting cases involving sepsis, stroke, autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screening, inbox drafting, and ambient documentation demonstrate how predictive, automated, and generative AI reorganize attention, work, and information. The chapter also identifies recurring failures, including alert fatigue, capacity mismatch, weak local validity, hidden workload, poor standardization, and dashboards without action. It argues that model performance alone cannot establish organizational value; leaders must evaluate changed care, workload, equity, resource use, and trust. AI is therefore neither a standalone strategy nor a magic solution. It is an amplifier whose contribution depends on the workflow, governance, response capacity, and quality-improvement discipline of the organization in which it operates.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has ushered in a revolutionary age, revolutionizing the conventional mode of education and learning. The review outlines the different applications of AI in education in terms of personalized learning and education technology. AI in education has transformed the learning paradigm. AI systems personalise learning, increasing student interest and success. This paradigm breaks down educational gaps and accommodates varied learning styles. Curriculum, content, and assessment all employ AI to automate administrative activities. Data protection, systemic biases, and connection deficiencies must be addressed. For ethical and equitable AI-augmented educational resource allocation, educators, policymakers, and technologists must collaborate. This paper offers a thorough analysis of the changing dynamics of AI in education, focusing on personalized learning and educational technology. This synthesis of current research and trends seeks to inform future advancements in the evolving symbiosis between AI and education, promoting a knowledgeable and progressive approach to AI integration in the educational domain.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Enterprises spend billions on artificial intelligence, yet half of new models never leave the sandbox. According to recent data, only forty-eight percent of pilot projects reach production within twelve months. David Ohnstad examines this deployment paradox, revealing why feedback loops and real-world data are essential to bridging the gap between heavy investment and actual enterprise value. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in healthcare. Radiology is one of the most active areas of clinical AI development. Despite substantial investments, many AI systems struggle to gain traction in clinical practice. The issues are rarely purely technical; they concern how AI tools fit into existing workflows, how they interact with professional responsibilities, and how they sit within institutional arrangements. It also remains unclear how core values in AI research such as explainability, value alignment, accountability, and trust are negotiated in clinical work. Established Health Technology Assessment (HTA) models define assessment domains but offer limited guidance on implementation: how technologies are staged within workflows, how responsibilities are redistributed, and how local conditions redefine value for different stakeholders. This paper presents the AI in PRACTICE framework, a five-phase methodology grounded in Techno-Anthropology and its relational ontology, for examining the situated work through which AI becomes part of clinical practice. Explainability, value alignment, trust, and distributed responsibility are understood as produced through socio-technical practices. The framework complements existing HTA models through iterative engagement and stakeholder participation. Insights are illustrated through three radiology-facing AI projects showing how assessment criteria are enacted, resisted, and revised in context, and how the framework generates practice-based artefacts.

documents.abstract: The proposed research centres on how artificial intelligence (AI) influences the choice of capital by foreign investors in ESG-related funds. It compares thirty funds across different regions using AI methods and traditional ESG funds. The results suggest that AI-based funds utilising machine learning and natural language processing show better financial results and stable risk-adjusted performance. Moreover, these technologies improve the quality of ESG disclosures and help detect inconsistencies, serving as a useful indicator of greenwashing cases. Regression analyses demonstrate a positive relationship between AI use and final fund performance. Great regional differences exist, with North America showing the highest integration. AI makes ESG investing more transparent and efficient, though regulatory frameworks are required.

The mismatch between Generation Z's (Gen Z) high expectations of artificial intelligence (AI) and organisational AI practices has profound implications for vocational well-being in India's job market. This research explores the structural path between Gen Z’s AI Expectations, Organisational AI Practices, and AI Literacy-Driven Vocational Well-being, with Skills Velocity as a key contextual variable in a rapidly changing, technology-driven landscape.This research used a mixed-methods approach. A structured questionnaire was administered to 203 Gen Z professionals and HR managers in AI-heavy industries (IT, BFSI and manufacturing) in Tier-1 and Tier-2 cities in India. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) using the lavaan package in R was used to test the path model. We triangulated our findings with 20 semi-structured interviews. The sample was skewed towards males (70:30 male-to-female) and non-normal.Based on the findings, the model fit was satisfactory. Gen Z's AI Expectations positively impacted Organisational AI Practices (β = 0.608, p < .001) and AI Literacy-driven Vocational Well-being (β = 0.449, p < .001). Organisational AI Practices also significantly and positively influenced Vocational Well-being (β = 0.418, p < .001). The variance in Organisational AI Practices and Vocational Well-being explained by the model was 36.9% and 60.4%, respectively.The research suggests that matching organisational AI practices to Gen Z expectations is crucial to improving AI literacy-based vocational well-being in India's ever-evolving labour market. The findings reveal the important role of Gen Z as a driver for change in organisations and the need for forward-looking, skills-velocity-sensitive human resource management strategies such as AI upskilling and training, ethical AI policies and lifelong learning opportunities to enhance retention and workforce preparedness.

documents.abstract: Abstract AI sycophancy is often conceptualized as a chatbot’s tendency to flout truth, accuracy, or other epistemic standards to shield users from hurt feelings, or otherwise protect them from the consequences of their thoughts, words, or actions. In this paper, I argue against this conception. That is, I argue that sycophantic AI behavior does not necessarily aim to protect users, nor that its harms are essentially epistemic . There are highly prevalent cases in which sycophantic AI chatbots actively contribute to their users’ knowledge. One class of such examples involves cases in which chatbots are used as auto-hermeneutic technologies —as tools to facilitate the user’s interpretation of her own cares, concerns, values, and other identity components and life events. In these cases, LLMs can help articulate the user’s avowed self-interpretations. In turn, avowals of these interpretations by users can often have downstream effects that render the interpretations true. If this is correct, then LLMs can often advance the user’s knowledge regarding important truths about herself. Simultaneously, as I explain, interpretations offered by LLMs may be deeply harmful. This understanding of AI sycophancy can help us clarify what is so disturbing about it, as well as resist the temptation to draw too tight an analogy between sycophantic behaviors in AI systems and in humans.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom has revolutionized the production of teaching content. However, the ideological implications of AI-generated content have been markedly under-researched in non-Western contexts. This study employs Fairclough’s three-dimensional framework of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) on a corpus of 45 AI-generated EFL reading texts produced by the ChatGPT-4o, Google Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Microsoft Copilot in response to five standardized instructional prompts. It aims to investigate how gender and Arab cultural identity is discursively constructed in materials targeting Gulf university EFL learners. Analysis of the findings show that the female professional is consistently represented through discourse of relational and communal achievement while the single male professional is coded through individual enterprise and resilience. Leadership discourse universalizes the individual while entirely erasing gender and cultural identity across the nine texts. Furthermore, a Western nuclear family development narrative renders the Arab family invisible. Finally, Microsoft Copilot shows the lowest cultural specificity and the highest degree of textual cloning across platforms. The findings further affirm that L2 writing created by these AI models replicates Western liberal ideological formations, thus marginalizing the cultural and gender identities of the Arab learners. The research makes pedagogical, technological, and policy recommendations for the culturally responsive use of AI tools in higher education in the Gulf.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students as a learning resource in STEM courses. However, classroom observations and survey data suggest that unstructured AI use may correlate with reduced student achievement. Two concerns are especially relevant: AI systems can produce incorrect responses in tasks requiring precise validation, and students may use AI in ways that reduce active engagement with course material. This session presents two instructional approaches designed to address these limitations: structured AI-generated worksheets and in-chat AI tutors. AI worksheets generate controlled sets of practice problems within instructor-defined course constraints. In-chat tutors provide interactive practice through problem generation, Socratic questioning, and feedback-driven guidance. The usefulness of each approach depends on the structure of the learning task. Drawing from iterative development and testing primarily in introductory chemistry, we examine four types of tasks: (1) conceptual and explanatory, (2) structured tasks with low ambiguity, (3) multi-step quantitative tasks, and (4) highly deterministic symbolic or structural tasks. Examples from chemical nomenclature, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, Lewis structures, laboratory writing, and mathematical validation illustrate where different AI approaches worked reliably—and where they did not. Participants will receive ready-to-use prompts for both AI worksheet systems and in-chat tutors, along with implementation strategies and observed limitations. The session concludes with a practical framework for selecting AI tools based on the structure of the learning task rather than disciplinary content alone.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: AI agents are becoming a new category of enterprise workforce alongside employees, contractors, softwarerobots, and traditional applications. As organizations assign AI systems persistent responsibilities, access rights, service expectations, and decision authority, workforce governance must expand beyond human resource management and technology operations. This paper proposes an AI Workforce Governance Framework that defines how enterprises should classify digital workers, assign ownership, establish roles and decision rights, manage identity and access, define supervision models, measure performance, control risk, govern collaboration with humans, and retire AI workforce components. The framework integrates enterprise architecture, operating model design, cybersecurity, Responsible AI, process governance, workforce transformation, and portfolio management. It enables organizations to treat AI agents as governed digital roles rather than uncontrolled automation, supporting productivity and innovation while maintaining accountability, transparency, human authority, and organizational resilience

documents.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and agent-based architectures have introduced new possibilities for automating web application security testing. Unlike traditional vulnerability scanners that rely mainly on signature-based detection, LLM-powered agents can analyze application context and dynamically adapt testing strategies. This exploratory case study examined two specific laboratory-defined workflows for identifying web application security weaknesses: a human-supervised agent-based workflow and a conventional vulnerability scanner workflow. The evaluation was performed in a controlled laboratory environment against the same target application and predefined ground truth, while each workflow retained its respective application-access, discovery, and authentication mechanisms. The agent-based framework was developed using Claude Code, the Model Context Protocol, and Burp Suite Professional, while the scanner-based approach utilized Qualys Web Application Scanning. Results were mapped to a predefined ground truth covering SQL Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, and Broken Access Control and reported using Recall, Precision, and false-positive counts where estimable. The findings describe what each completed workflow showed under the tested conditions, including coverage, tester effort, and validation workload, and outline directions for further evaluation.

What do well-informed students say about the use and integration of AI in their college educations? In Spring and Summer 2026 semesters, students in three sections of ENG 102 at UNR wrote AI-aware white papers with policy recommendations for the integration of genAI into higher education. To develop white paper policies, students read a variety of scholarly, public, and popular sources that show a variety of perspectives on Generative AI and LLMs, including the environmental and cognitive impacts. Then they considered the values and concerns of their audiences—peers, professors, and/or university administrators—to propose “sensible, well-informed, and well-reasoned” policies. This session will discuss their recommendations, insights, and the somewhat surprising classroom experience of teaching sustained, critical enquiry about Generative AI.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Climate change has intensified the frequency and severity of urban flooding, creating unprecedented challenges for municipalities worldwide. This study develops an AI-based decision-making framework that integrates machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and geospatial analytics to enhance urban flood risk management and resilience planning. The framework employs ensemble machine learning algorithms including Random Forest, XG Boost, and Cat Boost for flood susceptibility mapping, coupled with SHAP-based interpretability to decode model predictions and translate them into actionable policy insights at administrative scales. A city-scale digital twin component enables real-time flood impact simulation and cascading infrastructure disruption analysis, while a multi-criteria decision support module prioritizes adaptation investments based on economic risk assessment and equity considerations. The framework was validated using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SAR data and hydrological records across diverse urban environments, demonstrating superior predictive performance with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values exceeding 0.95 for ensemble models. Results reveal that elevation, proximity to hydrological features, and impervious surface density consistently emerge as dominant flood drivers, with their relative importance varying significantly across districts. The decision support system successfully transformed pixel-level predictions into ward-level actionable recommendations, enabling evidence-based zoning, drainage infrastructure prioritization, and targeted nature-based solutions deployment. The framework addresses critical gaps in explainability, scalability, and policy relevance that have limited the operational adoption of AI in urban flood governance. The study concludes that integrating AI-driven analytics with participatory decision-making processes can substantially enhance adaptive capacity in flood-prone urban systems, though algorithmic transparency, data equity, and institutional readiness remain essential preconditions for equitable implementation.

Anemia is a common disease that may occur in individuals due to low levels of hemoglobin in the blood, whereas conventional diagnosis usually requires clinical examination and laboratory tests. Preliminary screening is often hindered by economic, availability, and even early recognition challenges. AnemiaVision is the proposed artificial intelligence system designed to recognize potential cases of anemia from conjunctiva images. AnemiaVision uses a Convolutional Neural Network to process and classify the image data into anemic and non-anemic classes. The model was trained using a dataset of conjunctiva images categorized into Anemic and Non-Anemic classes. The images were preprocessed and normalized before model training. AnemiaVision is comprised of the trained model and a web interface, which allows users to upload a conjunctiva image and receive screening results with model confidence. The system was implemented using Python programming language, TensorFlow/Keras framework, OpenCV computer vision library, and PHP web interface framework. The proposed system was experimentally evaluated, and results showed potential for rapid preliminary screening of anemia. AnemiaVision is proposed as an educational and screening tool, which cannot substitute laboratory tests and clinical diagnosis by medical professionals.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a necessary technology to optimize High-Performance computers (HPC) systems and intelligent network architecture, such as optimizing the use of resources, the schedulization of workloads and network efficiency. This paper discusses how the three AI-based optimization tools, i.e., Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) can be optimized to enhance performance in the HPC environment. It was done using a quantitative, simulation based, approach on the benchmark HPC workload and HPC network datasets. Data cleaning, feature selection, normalization and train-test splitting were used to preprocess the datasets and then model implementation and evaluation took place. The models were evaluated based on performance such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, execution time, resource consumption, throughput, latency as well as the energy consumption. Experimental results demonstrated that the DRL model achieved the highest prediction accuracy of 96.8, 93.8 CPU resources consumption, 96.1 network efficiency, 12.8 Gbps throughput and 5.3 ms (lowest) network latency values. LSTM had the highest prediction accuracy of 95.2, and XGBoost had a score of 93.9 with the lowest training time rate of 39 minutes. The findings indicate that AI-based optimization is tremendously more effective regarding calculations and adaptability, scheduling, and resource allocation compared to the conventional ones. The suggested framework offers a viable solution to scalable, smart and energy efficient, intelligent HPC systems, which can be used to support next generations of computing and networking systems.

The proposed work develops a cost-effective IoT and artificial-intelligence-based predictive maintenance system for electric motor fault detection. A BO geared DC motor is monitored using an ESP32 microcontroller integrated with DHT11, INA219, and MPU9250 sensors to measure temperature, current, voltage, and vibration parameters. The collected sensor data are processed using time-domain statistical features and transmitted through Wi-Fi to a local server for analysis. Machine learning models, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost, are employed and combined using a soft-voting approach to improve fault classification. The system categorizes the motor condition into normal, highcurrent, and maintenance-required states. In addition, vibration, current, and temperature trends are analyzed to provide early warnings before critical thresholds are reached. Blynk IoT is used for remote monitoring, while automatic email notifications are generated when abnormal conditions persist. The study demonstrates the feasibility of implementing an affordable real-time predictive maintenance solution suitable for laboratories, small industries, and academic applications.

The increasing connectivity of industrial machines has changed maintenance from a largely schedule-driven activity into a continuous, data-driven process. Digital Twin (DT) technology supports this transition by providing a dynamic virtual representation of a physical asset that is continually updated using operational data. When artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded within the twin, the resulting system can move beyond visualization to support fault identification, anomaly detection, degradation assessment, Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation, and maintenance decision-making. This paper presents a structured review of AI-enabled digital twin approaches for predictive maintenance in smart manufacturing, examined end-to-end across physical sensing, data acquisition, communication, twin synchronization, intelligent analytics, maintenance decision-making, and remote corrective control. Machine learning, deep learning, unsupervised anomaly detection, hybrid and physics-informed models, edge intelligence, federated learning, and generative AI (GenAI) are discussed with respect to their industrial suitability and their bearing on the accessibility of digital-twin maintenance for resource-constrained manufacturers. Particular attention is given to a limitation that remains evident throughout the literature: most reported systems detect or predict abnormal behavior but stop short of converting those predictions into safe, closed-loop actions. The review classifies systems by their progression from monitoring and diagnosis to prediction, prescription, and autonomous control, and introduces a GenAI-Augmented Digital Twin Maturity Evaluation (GADT-ME) framework that scores a system jointly on functional maturity and generative-AI capability. Challenges relating to scarce failure data, latency, cybersecurity, synchronization, explainability, interoperability, computational cost, and deployment cost for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are also examined. The global Internet of Things (IoT) network has experienced unprecedented expansion, reaching 75.44 billion connected devices worldwide. Due to this rapid growth, the IoT ecosystem has become larger but also more vulnerable to various threats in cyberspace. As a result, this situation has accelerated the development of more complex cyberattacks, especially Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks, which can damage systems by overwhelming network traffic. This attack exploits the inherent vulnerabilities of IoT networks with limited resources, leading to significant service interruptions, monetary losses, and potentially the failure of vital infrastructures. As a result, this survey presents a new taxonomy of attack types, a thorough assessment of conventional and AI-driven detection techniques, and a comparison of advanced countermeasures. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic overview of DDoS attack detection, prevention, and mitigation approaches for the IoT. A major contribution of this work is the inclusion of blockchain-based security frameworks, federated learning, deep learning, machine learning, and quantum computing paradigms in its discussion for reducing DDoS attacks on the IoT. Furthermore, real-world case studies highlight the severe impact of such attacks on mission-critical domains, including smart cities, healthcare, and industrial control systems (ICSs). This survey provides a basis for cybersecurity researchers, security experts, and hobbyists, grounded in the understanding gained from previous research.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming education by enabling personalized learning pathways, automating tasks, and creating interactive technologies that expand access. Recent reports show that 87% of schools worldwide have adopted AI tools in some form, and the AI-in-education market is projected to grow from $5.88 billion in 2024 to $32.3 billion by 2030 ( Grand View Research, 2025 ; SQ Magazine, 2025 ). This review highlights how AI enhances individualized learning, improves student engagement, and streamlines administration. Simultaneously, challenges such as privacy risks, algorithmic bias, and the digital divide remain. Global frameworks from UNESCO emphasize that without strong ethical policies, AI can deepen inequalities rather than reduce them. This paper adopted a structural literature review approach that synthesized global reports, peer-reviewed studies, and policy documents to map out current trends. The paper concludes that AI&s;s potential in education can be realized only through responsible adoption, professional development for educators, and inclusive infrastructure investments. This paper integrates global adoption statistics with ethical and equity perspectives, highlighting the research gap in empirical classroom-based studies. These implications suggest that policymakers and educators must balance innovation with safeguards to ensure equitable outcomes.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization has increasingly transformed digital marketing by enabling firms to deliver individualized recommendations, content, and offers based on consumer data and behavioral patterns. However, the growing use of personalization also raises important questions regarding consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. This study aims to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) of research on AI-driven personalization in digital marketing to examine its implications for consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. Using Scopus as the primary database, the search process identified 2,906 records and, through successive filtering and screening procedures, resulted in 51 eligible studies. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and thematic synthesis were employed to identify publication trends, intellectual structures, and key research themes. The findings indicate a shift from technology-oriented research toward consumer-centered perspectives, with increasing attention to consumer experience, trust, engagement, privacy, transparency, purchase intention, and purchase behavior. The review further demonstrates that the effectiveness of AI-driven personalization is context-dependent and influenced by consumer perceptions and data-related concerns. These findings provide an integrated basis for understanding the evolving role of AI personalization in contemporary digital marketing

Abstract Public-sector building retrofits in the United Kingdom require decisions that balance whole-life cost, carbon reduction, service continuity and auditability under limited data and constrained capital budgets. This paper develops a decision-ready whole-life costing (WLC) workflow that integrates environmental, social and governance (ESG) priorities with uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence (AI) for public-building retrofit appraisal. The workflow combines national non-domestic Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) and Display Energy Certificate (DEC) data, Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) delivery evidence and stakeholder inputs to construct a scenario library of public-building archetypes, retrofit actions and appraisal constraints. Stakeholder priorities from interviews, a questionnaire and a co-design workshop are translated into transparent weights using fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (F-AHP). These weights parameterise a reinforcement learning (RL) planner, while a Bayesian convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (BCNN–LSTM) surrogate provides uncertainty-bounded energy, carbon and cost trajectories for repeated policy evaluation. Results show that the workflow supports auditable retrofit sequencing across archetype and budget conditions and improves composite ESG performance relative to conventional WLC-only, £/tCO 2 e and static multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) baselines. For 1000 matched archetype–budget cases, the trained deep Q-network (DQN) decision-search stage achieves a 30.03-fold speedup over traditional scalar feasible-sequence enumeration. The contribution is an integrated and explainable WLC–ESG–AI workflow for early-stage public retrofit decision support. The current validation remains based on public datasets and scenario-level evidence so future work should extend the framework using project-specific metered data, digital twins and live portfolio deployment.

Artificial intelligence has structurally transformed financial phishing, collapsing the cost of personalised attacks; India recorded 135,173 financial phishing attacks in H1 2024, a 175% rise over 2023. This chapter examines the convergence of AI-enabled phishing, student data vulnerability, and digital literacy deficits in India's skill-based educational institutions (ITIs, polytechnics, skill universities), a population absent from existing cybersecurity literature despite holding data regulated under the DPDP Act, 2023. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, the Digital Literacy Continuum, and Institutional Theory, it develops the Protection Gap construct and a Four-Layer Institutional Defence Model. A primary survey (N = 96, seven states) finds 66.7% encountered suspected phishing, mostly via WhatsApp; only 25.0% identified a genuine message; 59.4% were unaware of the DPDP Act; and 43.8% reported no explicit consent for Aadhaar/bank data. The chapter closes with recommendations for MeitY, AICTE, NSDC, and the Data Protection Board of India.

Abstract Wearable sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being used to quantify athlete movement, physiological response, training load, and recovery in field and laboratory settings. However, the practical value of these systems depends not only on the predictive capability of an algorithm but also on sensor validity, signal quality, hardware constraints, real-time processing, and the transferability of models across athletes and sports. This review examines the technical pipeline linking wearable electronic sensors to athlete-monitoring decisions, with particular attention to inertial measurement units, global navigation satellite systems, photoplethysmography, electrocardiography, electromyography, pressure sensing, and multimodal systems. It synthesizes evidence on signal conditioning, segmentation, feature engineering, classical machine learning, deep learning, sensor fusion, edge inference, and embedded implementation. Existing reviews indicate that wearable devices can support useful monitoring, but accuracy varies by metric, device, movement pattern, and validation setting; performance under controlled conditions should not be assumed to generalize to competition. Key challenges include motion artifacts, inconsistent protocols, small and imbalanced datasets, leakage between training and test sets, limited external validation, battery and communication constraints, privacy, and unclear decision thresholds. The review proposes a layered reference architecture and a validation framework that links engineering performance to sport-specific usefulness. Future research should prioritize synchronized multimodal datasets, athlete-independent testing, interpretable and uncertainty-aware models, energy-efficient edge AI, secure data governance, and transparent reporting. The article’s contribution is an engineering-oriented synthesis that connects sensor physics and embedded constraints with the needs of physical education and sports science. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the development of deepfake technology, enabling the creation of highly realistic fabricated audio, video, and visual content that closely resembles authentic media. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining an online survey of 47 Namibian internet users and a total of 12 key informants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on deepfake technologies by providing empirical evidence from Namibia and offering practical recommendations for enhancing digital literacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and improving institutional preparedness.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Radiological examinations increasingly leverage artificial intelligence to enhance diagnostic performance by compensating for expertise shortages, particularly in specialized interpretation. Despite academic AI models achieving compelling accuracy, adoption remains low. An objective, evidence-based examination of AI-guided clinical image interpretation seeks to expose the underlying reasons. The primary challenge lies not in accuracy but in fully automated analysis, especially for multimodal and multidimensional datasets. Introduction of uncertainty measures, image explainability, and real-world data reduce recognition to a decisive-supporting role—helping radiologists to detect previously unnoticed abnormalities—or even to precautionary analysis. Patients requesting precision medicine and therapy planning—and those at high risk of neglected pathology—stand to gain the greatest benefit. Relevant AI architecture considers imaging cues suitable for precision medicine or requiring additional methods to obtain interpretable images. Successful performance testing against an external, hidden reference dataset promotes vital user trust. Machine learning achieves best results where all potentially pathological abnormalities are identified and their presence virtually guaranteed, as in multi-class recognition. Data scarcity, however, impedes clinically relevant solutions. Explainability, essential for medical applications and clinical acceptance, extends simply beyond clinical decision support to provide saliency maps and, better still, clinically meaningful image regions or qualities. Attention maps may even bring a form of rule-based reasoning within reach. Clinical integration that reproduces the technical conditions under which model diagnostic measures are calculated raises the challenge of uncertainty quantification—a necessary condition for clinical decision support. Convolutional neural networks trained for photo-quality classification, par excellence supervised image quality assessment, provide the basic cues for uncertainty quantification. Imaging acquisition, modality, and systems are also defined in terms of current PACS/EPIC systems. PE, pre-symptomatic examination or precautionary examination, is defined as a patient-user group prepared to cover the cost of an examination with lower diagnostic accuracy and a high level of uncertainty.

documents.abstract: This repository accompanies the manuscript "When AI Speaks for Heritage: Algorithmic Visibility, Channel-Size Confounds, and the Authenticity Backlash in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage on YouTube", submitted to Telematics and Informatics Reports (Special Issue: Cultural Heritage and AI for Strategic Communication, Digital Innovation, and Global Engagement). **Data:** per-video metadata and final labels (videos_final_labels.csv), channel metadata, raw and labelled comment corpora, per-coder LLM labels, and the 31-video adjudication + 300-video human-validation records. **Prompts:** verbatim system/user prompts for all five LLM coders and the comment classifier. **Code:** the end-to-end pipeline from platform pull through labelling to analysis and validation; analysis.py reproduces every number in the manuscript. All data are publicly available YouTube metadata and public comments (no private data; no API keys committed; credentials read from environment variables). Licence: CC-0 (data), CC-BY-4.0 (code). Public from submission, no embargo.

The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) based robo-advisor has become a disruptive game-changer in the field of investment advisory service, altering the manner in which portfolios are managed as well as how individuals are making investing choices. These platforms provide cost-efficient, personalized and scalable financial recommendations using Big data analytics, machine learning, and algorithmic automation. The paper is a systematic literature review carried out with the help of PRISMA to draw generalizations on the available literature on the topic of AI-powered robo-advisors, the basics behind their technology, the impact on investor behavior, the performance of their portfolios, and the ethical and regulatory issues related to this field. Based on the searches of peer-reviewed published literature published in 2016-2025, the review determines the main themes in the context of decision accuracy, reduction of behavioral bias, risk optimization, and democratization of financial advice. The results reveal that the efficiency and objectiveness of investment management is considerably increased by robo-advisors, but the issues of data privacy, algorithmic transparency, and regulation are raised. The paper concludes that hybrid advisory models that integrate AI with the human judgment skills are the most sustainable future of the investment advisory services. New issues of data privacy, algorithmic transparency, ethical fairness, and regulatory compliance are critically looked into as well as those benefits such as automation, objectivity, accessibility and democratization of financial advice are identified. It argues in the study that hybrid models of advising that integrate AI capabilities with human decision-making will probably Explain the future of the investment guidance services utilising real case studies and research that is currently available.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for connecting research‐led teaching with authentic industry projects, yet its educational value depends on how educators organize inquiry rather than on technological use alone. This study examined the relationships among AI‐supported research‐led teaching (AIRLT), educator questioning (EQ), educator feedback (EF), student inquiry engagement (SIE), and authentic project learning outcomes (APLO) within Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 898 undergraduate students from 12 universities in Vietnam who had participated in authentic industry or organizational projects involving AI‐supported inquiry and educator guidance. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) showed that AIRLT was positively associated with EQ ( β = 0.642) and EF ( β = 0.611). Both EQ ( β = 0.463) and EF ( β = 0.349) were positively associated with SIE, which, in turn, showed a strong positive association with APLO ( β = 0.689). All six specific indirect effects were significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations among AI‐supported teaching, educator guidance, student inquiry, and perceived authentic learning outcomes. The findings contribute an educator‐mediated perspective to Syntegrative Education by showing that AI is most educationally meaningful when embedded in purposeful questioning, feedback, and sustained student inquiry. The study highlights the importance of designing AI‐supported industry projects around evidence evaluation, iterative feedback, reflection, and active investigation of authentic problems rather than treating AI use as an educational objective in itself.

ABSTRACT Firms increasingly incorporate generative and non‐generative artificial intelligence (AI) into product design, formulation, and production, and they face a disclosure question: how should they describe the role of AI to consumers? Across six studies, including analysis of 1800 marketplace listings and five pre‐registered experiments (total experimental N = 2760), we introduce and test a 2‐by‐2 framework of algorithmic provenance defined by the AI's role (agentic vs. assistive) and its visibility in the final product (visible vs. invisible). Identical products are evaluated differently depending on where they fall in this taxonomy. Agentic AI involvement (AI as designer) reduces consumer product attitudes, perceived quality, purchase intentions, and willingness to pay relative to assistive AI involvement (AI as a tool for a human designer). The effect is amplified when AI involvement is visible in the final product. The downstream responses are partially mediated by a new construct, perceived authenticity of creative intention, which captures consumers' inference about whether a human creator pursued a genuine creative vision. The effect is larger for expressive than for functional product domains and larger among consumers primed to hold an independent self‐construal. A scalable managerial intervention, creative‐intent framing, narrows the agentic penalty by approximately half, again through the authenticity mechanism. The findings identify a substantively important new construct for AI disclosure research, refine theories of algorithmic aversion, and offer marketers an actionable disclosure design principle.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench

documents.abstract: Network-on-Chip (NoC) architectures have become a fundamental communication backbone for many-core processors, artificial intelligence accelerators, edge-computing platforms, and high-performance embedded systems. However, achieving efficient packet routing in large-scale NoCs remains challenging due to dynamic traffic variations, congestion propagation, limited global network visibility, and stringent hardware constraints. Conventional deterministic and heuristic routing algorithms suffer from reduced adaptability under non-uniform traffic conditions, whereas existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based routers primarily rely on local state representations and finite-state-machine (FSM) controllers, limiting their scalability, topology awareness, and hardware deployability. To address these limitations, this work proposes an Adaptive Congestion-Aware Graph Neural Routing Framework with Hybrid Microcoded Event-Driven Control for Network-on-Chip Systems. The proposed framework integrates three complementary components: (i) an Adaptive Congestion-Aware Graph Neural Network (ACA-GNN) encoder that generates compact topology-aware embeddings by capturing local and multi-hop congestion dependencies through congestion-aware message propagation, (ii) a quantized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent that performs low-latency adaptive routing decisions using compact graph embeddings, and (iii) a Hybrid Microcoded Event-Driven Controller (H-µEDC) that replaces conventional FSM-based control with programmable event-triggered micro-routines to ensure deterministic routing execution. The proposed architecture is implemented on a Xilinx Zynq-7000 FPGA and evaluated using BookSim2 cycle-accurate simulation, Orion 3.0 power modeling, synthetic traffic patterns, and PARSEC/Rodinia benchmark workloads. Experimental results demonstrate up to 48% lower packet latency, and 31% lower energy per flit compared with state-of-the-art heuristic and machine-learning-based routing approaches. Hardware implementation further requires only 1.2% LUTs, 1.4% flip-flops, three DSP blocks, one BRAM, and 0.556 W power consumption while maintaining deterministic single-cycle routing decisions using cached ACA-GNN embeddings. These results demonstrate that the proposed ACA-GNN-HµEDC framework effectively combines topology-aware routing intelligence, congestion adaptivity, hardware efficiency, and scalability, making it a practical solution for next-generation many-core Network-on-Chip systems.

Predicting student performance has become a vital objective in educational data mining, however existing models remain limited by limited feature sets, opaque decision processes, and the absence of real-time, context-aware interpretative intelligence. This study presents a novel hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) architecture that integrates cognitive, emotional, and general intelligence indicators with formative assessment/class performance data to construct a multidimensional demonstration of student performance. The system utilizes a mathematically formalized feature-weighting mechanism that allows domain experts to regulate the influence of key predictors prior to training, enabling a tunable and educator-configurable modeling process. Interaction between cognitive, emotional, and behavioral properties are explicitly engineered to capture complex effects often overlooked in prior research. An ensemble predictive model combining Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Linear Regression is used to predict student grades, with uncertainty measured through variance-based confidence intervals. The integrated system exhibited strong predictive capability, attaining high accuracy (R 2 = 0.9014, 95% CI [0.8882, 0.9121], 10,000 bootstrap resamples) with low prediction error, confirming the stability and reliability of the ensemble model. Understanding why a model produces a particular prediction is often as important as the prediction itself. To address the interpretability gap, the system incorporates SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based global and local explanations, a counterfactual simulation engine that estimates the marginal impact of improving specific attributes, and a local generative AI layer deployed via Ollama that creates these outputs into structured, real-time narrative feedback. Running the Large Language Model (LLM) locally ensures privacy-preserving, institution-compliant interpretability while permitting interactive, student specific explanations. This integration of predictive modeling, explainability, simulation, and local generative reasoning creates a unified decision-support framework that exceeds traditional black-box approaches. Experimental assessment shows that the model not only achieves viable predictive accuracy but also provides actionable insights into feature influence, model stability, and potential intervention pathways.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Wearable human–machine interfaces (HMIs) are at the forefront of next‐generation intelligent systems, demanding interfaces that are not only accurate and responsive, but also ergonomic, stretchable, and seamlessly integrated into daily life. In this work, we present a novel HMI system enabled by a glove and garment, based on fully textile, matrix‐free capacitive strain sensors (CSSs). Our sensor is fabricated via a single‐step, sewing‐machine‐compatible double‐twisted knitting process of silver‐coated knitted textile electrodes and a nylon/elastane textile dielectric, eliminating the need for post‐processing, polymer encapsulation, or rigid substrates. The resulting all‐fabric CSS demonstrates a high gauge factor of 2.03 over a broad strain range (0–72%), with excellent linearity (R 2 = 0.982), hysteresis (7.80%), and minimal signal creep. The textile‐based architecture preserves garment‐level wearability, with the nylon/elastane dielectric exhibiting a porosity of ∼66%, while the silver‐coated textile electrode (∼77% porosity) maintains a low and stable resistance (∼4.4 Ω) under 0–60% strain. Integrated into a wearable glove, the proposed system enables detection of 10 distinct hand gestures with recognition accuracy of 90.5%. This work marks a significant advancement toward fully textile‐integrated, breathable, comfortable, stretchable, and high‐performance HMI solutions, with broad implications for virtual environments, assistive technologies, and next‐generation wearable robotics.

documents.abstract: Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) models solve the gravitationally self-consistent sea-level equation for the response of the solid Earth and the oceans to changing ice loads. As these models are increasingly embedded in coupled ice-sheet simulations, glacial-cycle calculations, and large ensembles, standard pseudo-spectral 1-D solvers face a steep computational barrier: they evaluate the viscoelastic response by explicitly re-summing every past load increment, scaling quadratically with time steps as $O(N^2)$. Here we show that this computational penalty is an artifact of algorithmic formulation rather than Earth physics. By exploiting the exponential form of the viscoelastic relaxation kernel, we reformulate the viscous response as an exact recursive update of a finite set of modal states, without re-summing the load history. This exact reformulation alone reduces the cost of a run to $O(N)$, yielding a 20.6-fold speed-up relative to a standard full-history 1-D GIA solver for a case study involving a 550-step Antarctic future sea-level projection. Implemented in our open-source solver SLEvolve v1.0, this formulation---combined with fewer, table-free and multithreaded spherical-harmonic transforms, improved file handling, and physics-inspired iteration starts---achieves an end-to-end speed-up of over three orders of magnitude (up to 4,000-fold) against the same 1-D GIA solver, reducing day-long simulations to under thirty seconds on a workstation. Beyond this solid-Earth application, SLEvolve illustrates how human-derived analytical reformulations can be combined with benchmark-harnessed AI-assisted engineering to modernize scientific software. In particular, Numerical regression tests and performance profiling guided the AI agents' implementation choices and helped reject ineffective optimizations.

documents.abstract: The new materials industry is a strategic pillar industry underpinning China's pursuit of technological self-reliance and self-strengthening. It plays a vital role in the development of advanced manufacturing, the achievement of the "dual carbon" goals, and the security of industrial and supply chains. The deep integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with materials Research and Development (R&D) is continuously reshaping the innovation and production models of the industry. Existing literature has extensively examined new materials technologies and AI-driven innovation, but relatively little research has systematically analyzed the competitive landscape of the industry from the perspective of industrial economics. Clarifying the characteristics of industry competition can provide practical insights for domestic industrial policymaking and overseas industrial deployment under the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative. Using Porter's Five Forces model as the analytical framework, this study examines the competitive characteristics of China's new materials industry by drawing on publicly available industry reports, existing literature, and online interviews with industry practitioners, given the constraints on obtaining first-hand corporate research samples. The findings indicate that the industry as a whole has high entry barriers, while supplier bargaining power varies significantly across different segments. Buyers and substitutes exert moderate competitive pressure, and the intensity of intra-industry competition differs substantially between low-end and high-end segments. Based on these findings, corresponding industrial policy recommendations are proposed, followed by a discussion of the limitations of this study and directions for future research.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on audio-visual question answering, but correct answers do not necessarily imply that their stated reasoning is grounded in relevant perceptual evidence. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final-answer accuracy, offering limited insight into whether model-generated rationales correctly identify visual regions, temporal intervals, and audio events supporting predictions. We introduce ANCHOR, a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring grounded-rationale alignment in multimodal reasoning, comprising 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs with structured reasoning traces, temporal evidence, spatial bounding boxes, and salient audio cues, including a human-refined test set of 224 videos and 975 question-answer pairs. We separately measure answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, and conciseness, with direct spatial and temporal grounding measurements on a focused subset. Across the full benchmark, twelve contemporary MLLMs show a substantial alignment gap: models with comparable answer performance can differ markedly in whether their explanations are supported by annotated evidence. On a matched subset of 100 videos and 446 question-answer pairs, rankings remain highly stable across human-refined, Gemini-generated, and GPT-generated references (mean Pearson r=0.99), providing evidence against model-reference circularity within this subset. Grounding-cue ablations of three MLLMs on the full human-refined test set reveal a consistent modality hierarchy: removing video reduces accuracy by 38.4-41.8 points, while removing bounding boxes (3.2-7.7 points) and audio (4.2-5.6 points) causes smaller, complementary, model-dependent drops. These findings show answer-only evaluation obscures important grounding failures and position ANCHOR as a testbed for evaluating accurate and evidence-aligned audio-visual reasoning.

Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $κ= 0.82$.
